facebook.long_form:
Carlos Alcaraz is in the ATP Finals final.

He beat Ben Shelton 3-6, 6-3, 7-6(1) on Saturday in Turin — but it did not come easy. Shelton won the first set, broke early, and played the kind of aggressive tennis that reminded everyone why he earned this semifinal spot. Alcaraz, who had been managing a left thigh issue all week, had to adjust.

He did. The second set was more like the Alcaraz we expect — sharp, moving well, putting pressure on every return. And then the tiebreak told the whole story: Alcaraz won it 7-1. No drama, no hesitation. When it matters most, he finds a way.

This is Alcaraz's first ATP Finals final. He enters the championship match having won 13 consecutive matches. He meets Alexander Zverev on Sunday.

For Shelton, this tournament was a genuine moment. He made it to his first ATP Finals semifinal, pushed the best player in the world to three sets, and left with a 2-2 record. That is not a disappointing result — that is growth.

Who do you think wins today — Alcaraz or Zverev?

facebook.long_form:
Alexander Zverev is into the ATP Finals final, and he has been utterly dominant in Turin.

He beat Daniil Medvedev 7-6(0), 6-4 on Saturday night — and the numbers tell the story better than words can. That tiebreak? Zverev won it 7-0. Not a point dropped. Medvedev, one of the best tiebreak players on tour, did not win a single point.

Five matches. Zero sets lost. That is Zverev's tournament record heading into Sunday's final. His serve has been massive, his movement crisp, and his decision-making close to flawless. The ankle concern he mentioned before the tournament — the one he said would "probably stay until the end of my career" — has not been a factor at all in his results.

Medvedev walked in with a 14-8 head-to-head advantage. Zverev treated that number like it did not exist. He is the year-end world No. 1, and right now, he is playing like it.

The final is today. Zverev vs Alcaraz. What do you think — can Alcaraz find a way, or does Zverev complete a perfect tournament?

stories.title: Alcaraz vs Zverev — The 2026 ATP Finals Final (3:00 PM CET)

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text: Alcaraz vs Zverev. ATP Finals final. Today. 3:00 PM CET. Alcaraz seeking his first title here. Zverev seeking his third (2018, 2021). One of them makes history this afternoon. #ATPFinals #Tennis #ATP #ATPFinals2026

facebook.long_form:
The 2026 Nitto ATP Finals final is today. Alcaraz vs Zverev. 3:00 PM CET at the Inalpi Arena in Turin.

It is the matchup tennis wanted. The year-end No. 1 against the sport's most dynamic player. Two different styles, two different stories to this week. Zverev has not dropped a set in five matches — a metronomic perfection. Alcaraz came from a set down to beat Shelton, managing a thigh issue throughout.

The head-to-head stands at 7-6 to Alcaraz overall, though Zverev holds the edge on hard courts. Their last meeting was the 2026 Australian Open semifinal — Alcaraz won in five sets. Finals are different. Surface matters. Big servers tend to do well at year-end championships, and Zverev's serve has been the best in the tournament this week.

What history is at stake: Alcaraz can become the first Spanish ATP Finals champion since Álex Corretja in 1998. Zverev can win his third title, joining a group of eight all-time greats who have done the same.

One final. Two stories. Who takes it?

stories.title: What an Alcaraz Title Would Mean — First ATP Finals Crown, First Spanish Champion Since Corretja

x_posts.label: Post 4
x_posts.text: If Alcaraz wins today, he becomes the first Spanish ATP Finals champion since Álex Corretja in 1998. 28 years. He has won Wimbledon twice, Roland Garros, the US Open. This is the last piece. #ATPFinals #Tennis #ATP #Alcaraz

facebook.long_form:
Carlos Alcaraz has won almost everything.

Two Wimbledon titles. Roland Garros. The US Open. At 23, he has a Grand Slam on every surface that holds one. But the ATP Finals — the year-end championship for the eight best players in the world — has never been his.

Until today, he had never even played in the final. The tournament structure has worked against him, the draw has not been kind, and injury has ended runs before they began. Now he is here, with a 13-match winning streak, managing a thigh concern, and facing the most in-form player of the week in Alexander Zverev.

If he wins, he completes a career sweep of the sport's biggest titles. He also becomes the first Spanish champion at the ATP Finals since Álex Corretja lifted the trophy in 1998 — 28 years ago.

That is what today is about for Alcaraz. History. The last piece.

Do you think he can do it?

stories.title: Zverev's Third Title Bid — World No. 1, Five Wins, No Sets Dropped

x_posts.label: Post 5
x_posts.text: Zverev is year-end No. 1. He hasn't dropped a set all week. If he wins today, he joins 7 others who have won the ATP Finals three or more times. The final starts in a few hours. #ATPFinals #Tennis #ATP #Zverev

facebook.long_form:
Alexander Zverev was already having a career-best year before this week. He finished as year-end world No. 1 for the first time in his career. Now he is in the ATP Finals final without dropping a set, with a chance to win the tournament for the third time.

The list of players who have won the ATP Finals three or more times is short. Ivan Lendl. Pete Sampras. Roger Federer. Novak Djokovic. Jimmy Connors. Ilie Nastase. John McEnroe. Lleyton Hewitt. Zverev already has two titles — 2018 and 2021. A third today would put him in that company.

He has looked the part all week. His serve is functioning at the highest level. His foot movement is sharp. The ankle that caused concern before the tournament has not cost him a single set, let alone a match.

The challenge is Alcaraz, who leads their head-to-head 7-6 and won their last meeting in a five-set Australian Open semifinal earlier this year. But hard-court finals often favor the big server, and Zverev's ball has been the best in Turin.

Can he finish it?
